# Best Laptop for Students Under 800 (Euro or Dollar) in 2026

Lenovo

 IdeaPad Slim 5 14 (Gen 9, AMD) 

 €650 $600 RRP 

Under 800, buy the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 14 (Gen 9, AMD). It is the only machine on this site that lands cleanly inside a real student budget and does not punish you for the price.

 Linux ok 9.9 Linux readiness 9.9 of 10, confidence high 16 GB soldered RAM 

Photo: EeveeRBL · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons (IdeaPad Slim family reference)

 Compiled & edited by Dennis de Kruijf · updated 2026-05-18 · how we rate 

## At a glance

| Laptop | CPU | RAM | Our score | RRP | Linux |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 14 (Gen 9, AMD) Our pick | AMD Ryzen 7 8845HS | 16 GB | 6.8 | €650 $600 | Linux ok |
| Apple MacBook Air 13 (M4) | Apple M4 (10-core) | 16 GB | 8.3 | €1,199 $999 | Linux gaps |
| Apple MacBook Air 13 (M3) | Apple M3 (8-core) | 8 GB | 8.2 | €1,299 $1,099 | Linux gaps |
| Framework Laptop 13 (AMD Ryzen 7040) | AMD Ryzen 7 7840U | 16 GB | 7.0 | €1,149 $1,099 | Linux ok |
| Dell XPS 13 9350 | Intel Core Ultra 7 258V | 16 GB | 7.2 | €1,599 $1,399 | Linux gaps |

Under 800, buy the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 14 (Gen 9, AMD). It is the only machine on this site that lands cleanly inside a real student budget and does not punish you for the price.

A note on the number first. Most “under 800” lists quietly mean dollars, then link a laptop that costs 850 euro after VAT. This guide uses the list price from our database. The IdeaPad is around 600 dollars or 650 euro at list, so it clears the bar in either currency with room for a case and a mouse. The other options here mostly do not, and we will say so plainly instead of pretending. Want the full field? Every model under 800 in our database, ranked.

## Our pick: IdeaPad Slim 5 14 (Gen 9, AMD)

Ryzen 7 8845HS, Radeon 780M, 16 GB RAM, an 84 Wh battery good for about 8 real hours. For 600 dollars that is a lot of machine. It handles a full course load: documents, browser with thirty tabs, a video lecture, light photo work, even some coding for an intro class. It will not edit 4K video and it is not trying to.

The honest downsides. The screen is a plain 300-nit 1920x1200 panel, fine indoors, washed out on a sunny library terrace. The keyboard is acceptable, not memorable. It weighs 1.45 kg, so not the lightest thing in a backpack. None of that is a flaw at this price. It is what 600 buys, and the parts that matter, the chip and the battery, are the parts they did not cut.

One more thing students should care about: this is one of the most trouble-free Linux machines in the budget class. If your university hands you a Windows licence you will never use, you can wipe it and run Ubuntu with almost no fuss on kernel 6.5 or newer. Check the exact Wi-Fi card on the unit you buy; that is the only variable.

## Runners-up and stretch options

MacBook Air 13 (M4), if you can stretch to about 999. This is over budget, no way around it. But if you can find the money, the M4 Air is the best student laptop made: 15 hours of real battery so you never carry a charger to campus, near-silent, and it will still be fast in your final year. 256 GB base storage is tight, so manage your downloads. If 800 is a hard ceiling, skip it. If it is a soft target, this is the one to save for.

MacBook Air 13 (M3). Often discounted now that the M4 exists. The trap is the 8 GB base RAM. macOS handles 8 GB better than Windows does, but for a four-year degree it is thin and you cannot upgrade it later. Only consider this on a steep sale, and only the 8 GB model if your work is genuinely light: notes, browser, streaming.

Framework Laptop 13 (AMD Ryzen 7040), the buy-once option. Around 1099 dollars, so well over budget, listed here for one reason. It is the most repairable laptop you can buy. Crack the screen in year two and you replace the screen, not the laptop. For a student who keeps a machine for six years, the lifetime cost can undercut buying two cheap laptops. Slotted RAM, runs Ubuntu LTS with almost no fuss. A long-game pick, not a budget one.

Dell XPS 13 9350. Premium build and 11-hour battery, around 1399 dollars. Out of budget and listed only to steer you off it on a student Linux setup: the webcam is broken on Linux from a Dell BIOS bug. For Windows-only students with money it is fine. For this guide, it is the wrong tool.

## What actually matters in a student laptop

- Battery you can trust through a teaching day. Eight real hours minimum so you are not hunting for a wall socket between lectures. The IdeaPad’s 84 Wh pack is the unsung hero of this pick.
- Enough RAM for a four-year horizon. 16 GB, not 8. Software bloats over a degree. 8 GB feels fine in first year and crawls by your thesis. This is the single reason to avoid the cheapest MacBook Air config.
- A keyboard and chassis that survive a backpack. You will carry this daily and treat it badly. Plastic that flexes is fine; hinges that loosen are not. The mainstream picks here are all built for daily abuse.
- The real price after tax, in your currency. A 750 dollar laptop is often 800 euro plus once VAT lands. Decide your true ceiling first, then shop. That is why the genuinely-under-800 list here is short and honest.

Screen quality and weight are where budget machines cut. Accept a plain panel and an extra 200 grams; do not accept thin RAM or a tired battery.

## FAQ

Is 600 dollars really enough for a laptop that lasts a degree? Yes, if you buy the right 600. The IdeaPad Slim 5 puts the money into the chip and battery and saves it on the screen. Those are the right places to cut for a student.

Should I buy a MacBook for university? Only if you can clear about 999 for the M4 Air, and never the 8 GB M3 at full price. The M4’s battery and longevity justify the stretch if the budget can bend. If 800 is firm, the IdeaPad is the answer.

Do I need a touchscreen or a 2-in-1 for taking notes? Most students who buy one stop using the tablet mode within a month. A normal laptop and a separate tablet, if you want one, is more reliable and usually cheaper than a convertible that compromises both modes.

Can I run Linux on a cheap student laptop? On the IdeaPad Slim 5, yes, easily. The all-AMD design is one of the most painless Linux platforms under 650, on kernel 6.5 or newer. Confirm the Wi-Fi card model before you buy.

Is 256 GB of storage enough? For cloud-first study with documents and streaming, yes. For a media or design course with large project files, no. If you pick a 256 GB MacBook, plan to live in the cloud and keep an external drive for backups.

Under 800, the IdeaPad Slim 5 is the call. If the budget can bend to about 999, save for the M4 Air instead. Everything between those two is a compromise you do not need.

# Best Engineering Laptops Under $1000 for Pros (2026)

 June 9, 2026 June 8, 2026 by Burak Boğa

## Key Takeaways

- Engineering laptops under $1000 now offer powerful performance due to advancements in AI chips and dedicated GPUs.
- Top picks include Lenovo LOQ 15, Acer Nitro V 16 AI, ASUS Zenbook A14 OLED, HP Victus 16, and Apple MacBook Air (M3).
- Key specifications to consider are RAM, CPU, and dedicated GPU for 3D modeling and simulations.
- Prioritize features that align with your major, whether it’s CAD-intensive or software-focused work.
- You don’t need to overspend; solid performance is available without exceeding the $1000 budget.

## Table of contents

- Quick Comparison: The Best Picks At A Glance
- Deep Dive: The Top 5 Engineering Laptops Under $1000

- 1. Lenovo LOQ 15 Gen 10 (AMD) — The Undisputed Budget Heavy-Lifter
- 2. Acer Nitro V 16 AI — The Best Value Screen Real Estate
- 3. ASUS Zenbook A14 OLED — The Dream Machine for Software Engineers
- 4. HP Victus 16 — The Sleek & Stealthy Professional
- 5. Apple MacBook Air (M3) — The Flawless Unix Workhorse
- Engineering Laptop Buying Guide: What Actually Matters?
- The Final Verdict
- How to Choose Your Perfect Engineering Laptop Under $1000
- Got Questions? We’ve Got Answers!

Look, let’s be totally honest here: engineering school or jumping into your first junior engineering gig is exhausting. Between running massive simulations in MATLAB, spinning up 3D models in SolidWorks, and compiling thousands of lines of code, your laptop takes a massive beating. That’s why finding the Best Engineering Laptops Under $1000 is so important for students and entry-level pros alike.

A few years ago, if you told someone you wanted a powerful engineering laptop for under $1000, they would have laughed and pointed you toward a $2,500 mobile workstation that weighs as much as a cinder block.

But it’s 2026, and things have completely changed. Thanks to hyper-efficient AI chips, entry-level dedicated GPUs that pack a massive punch, and competitive pricing wars, you can grab an absolute beast of a machine without draining your savings account.

Whether you are into mechanical, civil, electrical, or software engineering, here are the 5 best engineering laptops under $1000 that you can buy right now.

## Quick Comparison: The Best Picks At A Glance

Before we dive into the gritty details, here is a quick breakdown of our top contenders to help you spot your match instantly.

| Laptop Model | Best For | Core Specs (Under $1000 Config) | Standout Feature |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lenovo LOQ 15 Gen 10 | Heavy 3D Modeling & CAD | Ryzen 7, RTX 4060/5050, 16GB RAM | Bulletproof cooling systems |
| Acer Nitro V 16 AI | All-Round Raw Performance | Ryzen 7 AI, RTX 4060, 16GB RAM | Brilliant 16:10 display real estate |
| ASUS Zenbook A14 OLED | Coding & Software Engineering | Core Ultra 7 / Ryzen 7, Integrated Graphics, 16GB RAM | 15+ hour battery & gorgeous OLED screen |
| HP Victus 16 | Stealth Classroom Style | Intel Core i7, RTX 4050/4060, 16GB RAM | Clean, non-gamer aesthetic |
| Apple MacBook Air (M3) | iOS/Web Dev & Portability | Apple M3, 16GB Unified Memory, 512GB SSD | Incredible Unix ecosystem & feather-light |

## Deep Dive: The Top 5 Engineering Laptops Under $1000

### 1. Lenovo LOQ 15 Gen 10 (AMD) — The Undisputed Budget Heavy-Lifter

Lenovo LOQ Gaming Laptop

If your daily workload involves rendering assemblies, running structural analyses, or anything that makes a laptop fan scream, the Lenovo LOQ 15 is your best bet. Lenovo took everything that makes their premium Legion lineup incredible and stripped away the expensive bells and whistles to give you raw, unfiltered performance for under a grand.

#### Key Specifications

- Processor: AMD Ryzen 7 8845HS (or latest Ryzen AI equivalent)
- Graphics: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 / RTX 5050 (8GB/6GB VRAM)
- Memory: 16GB DDR5 RAM (Upgradable)
- Storage: 512GB / 1TB NVMe PCIe SSD
- Display: 15.6-inch FHD (1920×1080) 144Hz IPS

The Good:

- Thermal King: It stays surprisingly cool under heavy simulation stress thanks to its dual-fan rear-vent layout. No thermal throttling here.
- GPU Power: Getting a proper RTX card with dedicated VRAM at this price means your CAD viewports will render smoothly without stuttering.
- Upgradability: Unlike thin laptops, you can easily pop the back cover off later to add more RAM or a second SSD when your projects get bigger.

The Bad:

- Chunky Brick: It feels heavy in a backpack, and the power brick is quite large.
- Battery Life: Don’t expect to sit away from an outlet for more than 4–5 hours of regular use.

### 2. Acer Nitro V 16 AI — The Best Value Screen Real Estate

acer Nitro V 16 AI Gaming Laptop

Coding or designing structures on a cramped screen is a one-way ticket to an eye strain headache. The Acer Nitro V 16 fixes this by packing a gorgeous 16:10 aspect ratio display. This extra vertical space means you can see more lines of code or a larger canvas in AutoCAD without constantly scrolling.

#### Key Specifications

- Processor: AMD Ryzen 7 AI-enabled processor
- Graphics: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 (8GB VRAM)
- Memory: 16GB DDR5 RAM
- Storage: 1TB NVMe SSD
- Display: 16-inch WUXGA (1920×1200) 165Hz (16:10 Ratio)

The Good:

- The 16:10 Screen: Seriously, the extra vertical room is a game-changer for reading schematics and datasheets.
- Generous Storage: Comes out of the box with 1TB of fast storage, leaving plenty of room for heavy software packages like Ansys, MATLAB, and IDEs.
- Loads of Ports: Features an excellent selection of Type-C, HDMI, and ethernet ports—no dongles required in the lab.

- Plastic Build: The chassis is entirely plastic. It’s sturdy enough, but it doesn’t give you that premium aluminum feel.
- Pre-installed Bloatware: You’ll need to spend about 20 minutes deleting random pre-installed apps when you first boot it up.

### 3. ASUS Zenbook A14 OLED — The Dream Machine for Software Engineers

ASUS Zenbook A14 Copilot+ PC AI Business Laptop

Are you a computer science major or a software engineering student? Skip the bulky gaming rigs. You don’t need a massive graphics card to compile Python or Java. Instead, prioritize battery life, a stellar keyboard, and a display that won’t ruin your eyes during 3 AM debugging marathons. The Zenbook A14 is an absolute masterpiece for this.

#### Key Specifications

- Processor: Intel Core Ultra 7 or AMD Ryzen 7 8840HS
- Graphics: Intel Arc / AMD Radeon 780M (Integrated)
- Memory: 16GB LPDDR5X
- Storage: 1TB NVMe SSD
- Display: 14-inch 2.8K (2880×1800) 120Hz OLED Touchscreen

The Good:

- Mind-Blowing Display: The 2.8K OLED screen is shockingly crisp. Text looks razor-sharp, which reduces eye fatigue when coding for hours.
- Battery for Days: It easily lasts 12 to 15 hours on a single charge. You can leave the charger in your dorm room or home office all day.
- Ultra-Premium Portability: Aluminum lid, thin profile, and weighs under 3 pounds. It slides into any bag effortlessly.

- Integrated Graphics Only: It will struggle with intense 3D rendering or complex mechanical modeling. If you’re Mech-E or Civil, this isn’t for you.
- Soldered RAM: You cannot upgrade the memory down the road, so make sure you purchase the 16GB configuration.

### 4. HP Victus 16 — The Sleek & Stealthy Professional

HP Victus 15 Gaming Laptop

If you want the raw power of a gaming machine but don’t want to walk into a professional engineering firm or a lecture hall with a laptop flashing bright neon RGB lights, the HP Victus 16 is your answer. It looks like a high-end business ultrabook but hides serious hardware under the hood.

#### Key Specifications

- Processor: Intel Core i7-13650HX or newer Intel Core Ultra 5
- Graphics: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4050 / 4060
- Memory: 16GB DDR5 RAM
- Storage: 512GB PCIe Gen4 NVMe SSD
- Display: 16.1-inch FHD (1920×1080) 144Hz IPS

- Clean Design: Minimalist lines, clean branding, and a subtle white keyboard backlight. It fits right into any corporate setting.
- Excellent Keyboard: Features a full number pad, which is incredibly useful for entering coordinate data or crunching numbers in Excel.
- Quiet Mode: The cooling software has a fantastic quiet preset that keeps the fans silent during simple tasks like web browsing or writing documentation.

- Screen Flex: The display lid has a bit of wobble if you type aggressively or work on an unstable surface.
- Average Battery: Expect around 5 hours of moderate use before needing a plug.

### 5. Apple MacBook Air (M3) — The Flawless Unix Workhorse

Apple MacBook Air (M3)

Yes, a Mac can absolutely be an engineering laptop—with a huge catch. If you are focused on software engineering, web development, data science, or mobile app development (especially iOS apps), the MacBook Air with the M3 chip is a golden standard. Just make sure to look for deals or student discounts that drop the 16GB RAM configuration under $1000.

#### Key Specifications

- Processor: Apple M3 Chip (8-core CPU / 10-core GPU)
- Graphics: Integrated 10-core Apple GPU
- Memory: 16GB Unified Memory (Do not buy the 8GB version!)
- Storage: 512GB SSD
- Display: 13.6-inch Liquid Retina Display

- The Unix Ecosystem: macOS is built on Unix, meaning setting up developer environments, local servers, and terminal workflows is incredibly smooth.
- Build Quality: The trackpad, keyboard, and aluminum unibody build are miles ahead of any budget Windows laptop.
- Silent & Cool: It is completely fanless. It runs 100% silently, no matter how hard you push it, and never gets hot on your lap.

- Software Incompatibility: Major engineering software like SolidWorks, Autodesk Inventor, and Revit do not run natively on macOS. If your course requires these, stick to Windows.
- Zero Upgrades: What you buy is what you keep forever. No swapping components.

## Engineering Laptop Buying Guide: What Actually Matters?

Don’t get blinded by marketing jargon or glowing RGB lights. When shopping around the $1000 mark, focus heavily on these three pillars:

- RAM is King: Never buy a laptop with 8GB of RAM for engineering in 2026. 16GB is the absolute bare minimum for multitasking across CAD tools, IDEs, and 50 open Chrome tabs of documentation.
- Know Your Major: * Mechanical/Civil/Aerospace: You need a dedicated GPU (NVIDIA RTX or AMD Radeon discrete) for heavy 3D viewports.

- Software/Electrical/Chemical: You can prioritize a lighter chassis, longer battery life, and a better CPU over a heavy graphics card.
- Don’t Cheap Out on the CPU: Look for AMD Ryzen 7 (HS or HX series) or Intel Core i7 / Core Ultra 7. Avoid low-power variants (like Intel’s U-series or entry-level i3/Ryzen 3 chips) because they will choke during heavy calculations.

## The Final Verdict

If you want the absolute most power for your money to crush 3D models and simulations, grab the Lenovo LOQ 15. It’s a bulletproof workhorse that won’t let you down.

If you are a coder who values mobility, thin profiles, and jaw-dropping battery life, go for the ASUS Zenbook A14 OLED or the MacBook Air M3 (provided you don’t need Windows-exclusive CAD software).

Whichever you choose, every single machine on this list proves you don’t need to spend a fortune to get top-tier engineering performance. Find the one that matches your workflow, grab that student discount if you can, and get to creating!

## How to Choose Your Perfect Engineering Laptop Under $1000

Time needed: 5 minutes

1. Identify Your Core Engineering Software Requirements

Take a quick look at your syllabus or project list before spending a single dollar. If your work relies heavily on 3D modeling and stress-testing simulations (like SolidWorks, AutoCAD, or Ansys), you absolutely must prioritize a laptop with a dedicated graphics card like an NVIDIA RTX. If you are mostly writing code, compiling programs, or working with web tools, you can skip the heavy graphics card entirely and focus on getting the fastest processor and best battery life possible.
2. Lock Down Your Hardware Minimums (RAM & CPU)

Do not compromise on the internals just to save fifty bucks. Make sure the configuration you add to your cart has at least 16GB of RAM—8GB will choke and lag the moment you open a CAD tool alongside a dozen browser tabs. For the processor, look for an AMD Ryzen 7 or Intel Core i7 (or Core Ultra 7) from the last two generations so your machine has the processing muscle to handle heavy computational loads without crashing.
3. Balance Portability Against Desktop Power

Be realistic about your daily routine. If you plan to carry your laptop around campus or between client meetings all day, look for a slim, lightweight option like an ultrabook that offers over 10 hours of battery life so you aren’t tethered to a wall outlet. On the other hand, if you don’t mind a heavier backpack and want a machine that acts as a true desktop replacement for heavy rendering, go for a slightly thicker budget gaming chassis that features robust cooling fans.

## Got Questions? We’ve Got Answers!

Choosing a laptop for engineering can feel like a high-stakes decision, and it’s completely normal to have a few lingering doubts. Here are three of the most common questions we get from readers trying to get the best bang for their buck.

1. Is 16GB of RAM really enough for engineering in 2026, or should I stretch my budget for 32GB?

For most students and junior engineers, 16GB is still the sweet spot and will handle your CAD models, coding environments, and daily multitasking beautifully. However, if your budget allows for a laptop with upgradeable memory (like the Lenovo LOQ or HP Victus), you can comfortably buy the 16GB version now and cheaply pop in another 16GB stick a year or two down the road if you start running massive, complex simulations.

2. Can I use an affordable gaming laptop as a serious engineering workstation?

Absolutely! In fact, at the under-$1000 price point, budget gaming laptops are usually your best option for heavy engineering work. Gaming laptops are purposely built to handle intense graphic rendering and heavy processing loads, and they come with robust internal cooling systems. The only real downside is that they look a bit flashy and their battery life tends to be shorter than a standard office laptop.

3. What happens if I buy a Mac and my professor requires Windows-only software?

This is a super common headache. If you end up needing Windows-exclusive software like SolidWorks or Revit, running them on a modern Apple Silicon Mac can be incredibly frustrating. While tools like Parallels Desktop allow you to run Windows inside macOS, it can drain your battery and slow down your system. If your engineering department explicitly states you’ll be using Windows-based CAD programs, we strongly recommend sticking to a Windows machine to save yourself the tech-support stress.

Engineering Laptops provides in-depth laptop reviews, performance benchmarks, buying guides, and expert recommendations to help you choose the best laptop for work, study, gaming, and content creation.

# The Best Laptops for College Students

Laptops for college should be portable, offer long battery life, and be well priced. Based on testing hundreds of laptops, these are my top picks.

Courtesy of Apple

College laptops don’t have to be embarrassing. Nor do they have to be overly expensive. There are a lot of great, well-designed laptops for college students that combine long battery life, easy portability, and the performance needed for everyday coursework.

In my decade-plus of reviewing laptops, I’ve tested hundreds of models. If someone asked me what to buy for a college student, these are the ones I’d suggest.

Be sure to check out our other computing guides, including the Best Laptops, Best Budget Laptops, Best MacBooks, Best Windows Laptops, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Chromebooks, and Best Laptop Bags.

Updated July 2026: I’ve added the HP OmniBook 3 and Dell 14 Plus as picks, and the Dell 14S as an honorable mention. I’ve also removed some options that have become too expensive after price increases.

- The Best Overall College Laptop
- The Best Windows Alternative
- A Featherlight College Laptop
- The Best Cheap College Laptop
- The Best College Laptop Under $500
- Best Powerful College Laptops for STEM
- Other Laptops to Consider for College
- Do You Need a Laptop for College
- What Kind of Laptop Is Best for College?
- Are Chromebooks a Good Option for College?

## The Best Overall College Laptop

- Photograph: Luke Larsen
- Photograph: Luke Larsen
- Photograph: Luke Larsen
- Photograph: Luke Larsen

Apple

### MacBook Neo

Apple

The MacBook Air (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is my choice for best overall laptop for everyone. But college students have specific needs—and often, specific budgets. In addition to being affordable, a college student’s laptop should be lightweight and easy to carry around. The MacBook Neo (7/10, WIRED Recommends) fits the bill perfectly. It’s only 2.7 pounds and starts at just $699. It also has a smaller display, which helps it fit on those tiny lecture-hall desks. What makes the MacBook Neo special, however, is its lack of compromise around quality. It’s a gorgeous piece of hardware, with fun colors, an excellent trackpad, a beautiful display, and that Apple “it” factor. I recommend the $699 model, which gets you twice the storage and a Touch ID fingerprint reader.

Of course, this isn’t a laptop without downsides. Apple invested its efforts in the front-of-screen experience, but made cuts to performance, ports, and memory to keep costs low. The limitation of 8 GB of memory is my biggest sticking point with this device; it means you’ll need to be mindful of how many applications, tabs, and background tasks you have running at once. Also, ghe Neo can connect to only one external display at a time.

Dell

### 14 Plus

Dell (512 GB)

Laptop pricing has skyrocketed over the past few months, which has made it harder to recommend some of the flashier new laptops of the year. Fortunately, many really great laptops from 2025 are still available to buy. The Dell 14 Plus is a great example. It’s one of the few laptops you can get for less than $1,000 that doesn’t force you to make serious compromises. It’s not the world’s prettiest device, but the display is surprisingly sharp, bright, and colorful. The computer’s touchpad and keyboard are both high-quality, and it has tons of ports.

The newer Dell 14S came out more recently with the intention to replace the 14 Plus. The new model comes with an OLED display and superb battery life. While it’s a solid option (see Other Laptops to Consider, below), it starts at a pricey $1,350, and the screen has a lower resolution. For a college student, the Dell 14 Plus is the better buy right now.

## A Featherlight College Laptop

Asus

### Zenbook A14

If the idea of buying a laptop with only 8 GB of RAM in 2026 seems questionable (I don’t blame you for feeling this way), I recommend the Asus Zenbook A14 (WIRED Recommends, 8/10). Not only does it come with 16 GB of RAM, but it’s the lightest laptop you can buy right now at just 2.4 pounds. You’ll hardly notice it in your laptop bag when you’re trekking across campus.

The price of the Zenbook A14 varies quite a bit, typically between $600 and $1,000, but there’s often a deal available that makes it an affordable option. There’s also the 2026 model, which comes with the second-gen Snapdragon X2 chip. At $1,600, though, it’s just not worth the extra cash—especially for a college student on a budget.

## The Best Cheap College Laptop

HP

### OmniBook 5

The options listed above are fairly affordable, all coming in at less than $1,000. But even if your budget is $600 or less, trust that you can still get a solidly performing laptop with good battery life. The HP OmniBook 5 frequently sells for around $600 or less, making it an adequate MacBook Neo alternative. Better yet, HP’s laptop ships with more memory and storage. The OLED panel display is fantastic too, and the laptop is remarkably thin. The only significant downside is the touchpad, which feels clumsy to use. I could get used to it over time, but it is the Achilles’ heel of this OmniBook 5 (and nearly all budget laptops, for that matter).

- Photograph: Luke Larsen
- Photograph: Luke Larsen
- Photograph: Luke Larsen

HP

### OmniBook 3 (2026)

If you need a super-cheap Windows laptop, though, there’s really only one I’d recommend that’s cheaper than the OmniBook 5, and it comes from the same family. I tested the HP OmniBook 3 and found that it shares a lot of the positive qualities of its older sibling. The OLED screen is great, as is the keyboard and overall build quality. Most important, the battery life is top-notch for a device of this price. It’s not as thin as the OmniBook 5 though, and the 1920 x 1200 resolution stretched across the 16-inch screen is unfortunate. There’s also a 14-inch version, which I think is a smarter buy.

But there’s not a single other Windows laptop I’d feel good about suggesting someone buy at this price. Intel-powered laptops at this price tend to struggle with performance and battery life, while other cheap Qualcomm Snapdragon X laptops like the Asus Vivobook 14 use terrible displays to drag the prices down.

## The Best College Laptop Under $500

### Chromebook CX15

Chromebooks are becoming increasingly tough to sell. Snapdragon X-powered laptops like the HP OmniBook 3 above have made budget-tier Chromebooks, with weak battery life and poor screens, harder to justify. Furthermore, Chromebooks have the added problem of incompatibility with certain software you might need in college.

However, Chromebooks are still the way to go if you need something— anything—for as little money as possible. If you’re low on cash and just need basic internet access, the $200 Asus Chromebook CX15 is your best bet. The screen and touchpad are the main downfalls, but it’s fairly portable and modern-looking, and the battery life is decent enough. My bar is fairly low for a $200 laptop, but the CX15 outdoes other competitors at this price.

## Best Powerful College Laptops for STEM

### LOQ 15

Lenovo (RTX 5050, 512 GB)

Not everyone needs a powerful laptop to tote around campus. But if you’re in a STEM field, or even just like to play games on the weekend, buying a single, powerful laptop to serve as your main machine at college is a good idea. Unfortunately, no gaming laptop is powerful, portable, and affordable—you can only have two of those three things. Letting go of the portability priority, the best option I’ve tested is the Lenovo LOQ 15 (8/10, WIRED Recommends). It’s hard to beat a discrete graphics processing unit (GPU) for raw performance, which is exactly what the RTX 5060 in the LOQ 15 delivers. Though the price often creeps above $1,000, it’s still the most affordable gaming laptop you can buy that doesn’t suffer from severe performance compromises.

### Blade 16 (2025)

Razer

Now, if you can afford to dish out some more money, I’d point you to either the Razer Blade 16 or the MacBook Pro. Despite the thin profile of the Razer Blade 16 (8/10 WIRED Recommends), you can configure it with up to an RTX 5090 graphics card. Aside from the compromise of a high price, battery life is a limitation. You might run out halfway through your day, forcing you to find an outlet in a hurry. If you happen to need performance for gaming on the weekends in addition to your schoolwork, the Razer Blade 16 is expensive but totally worth it. I prefer the smaller Razer Blade 14 as a college laptop, but it’s no longer available to purchase right now.

The MacBook Pro, whether you opt for the M5 Pro, M5 Max, or an older chip, resolves the issue of battery life. Gaming isn’t its strongest capability, but it delivers exceptional performance in creative applications and can be equipped with up to 128 GB of unified memory for serious on-device AI workloads.

## Other Laptops to Consider for College

Photograph: Luke Larsen

Dell 14S for $1,350: While this laptop is more expensive than I’d like, it’s a solid choice. The chassis is more polished than that of the Dell 14 Plus, and the glossy OLED screen gives the device a premium look. I wish it were brighter, or at least handled glare better.

MacBook Air for $1,260: In previous years, the MacBook Air has been my top pick for college laptops, but in 2026, the prices and available configurations have gone up considerably. While it’s still overall the best laptop you can buy, the MacBook Neo is a better option for most college students, given its lower price.

Photograph: Luke Larsen

Apple iPad Air for $899: iPads can be solid laptop replacements, as long as you get the right one. The latest M4 iPad Air (7/10, WIRED Recommends) is the best example, as it’s not too expensive but still gives you the option of a larger, 13-inch display. The recent changes to iPadOS bring desktop-like multitasking to the platform, and when paired with a Magic Keyboard, you get a very capable 2-in-1 laptop. It’s an expensive accessory, but the keyboard and trackpad are both top-notch, on par with a high-end laptop.

Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x for $1,075: When it launched, this well-rounded, 15-inch laptop was selling for just $850. These days, it’s a few hundred dollars more, which is why I dropped it from a top pick to an honorable mention. The screen is brighter and more colorful than I expected, and even the touchpad feels smooth and responsive. It even gets excellent battery life and delivers a good balance between screen size and portability.

Microsoft Surface Pro 12

Photograph: Luke Larsen

Microsoft Surface Pro 12 for $750: I can’t think of a better device to bring to class for note-taking than the Surface Pro 12 (6/10, WIRED Recommends). While I recommend the larger Surface Pro 13 for most people, college students are the exception. The thinner and lighter size of the Surface Pro 12 gives you a super-portable Windows device. It has really solid hardware too. The Snapdragon X Plus provides just as much power and long-lasting battery life as the larger model. I wish it were a bit more affordable, as you’ll still need to add on the Surface keyboard and a USB-C power supply.

Framework Laptop 12 for $549: You can’t expect most budget laptops to last longer than four years of college. The Framework Laptop 12 (7/10, WIRED Recommends) promises something longer-lasting, as all Framework laptops do. This one is the smallest and cheapest in the lineup, and despite the price, the display and trackpad are both better than I expected. The only problem is the limited RAM.

Yes. Or, at the very least, some type of computing device you’re comfortable using. A laptop is still the preferred recommendation, but you could alternatively use a desktop in your dorm room paired with an iPad or a note-taking device in class.

The mobile aspect of a laptop makes it extremely easy to take your work with you between classes, while studying in coffee shops or typing notes in lecture, for example. Additionally, a laptop makes it easy to save space in cramped dorm rooms.

But as seen in my recommendations above, devices like the iPad Air and Surface Pro 12 could also be good solutions, as long as you pair them with their respective keyboard accessories.

All our guidelines for choosing a laptop also apply to college laptops, including evaluating the quality of the display and chassis, along with ensuring that the device is fast enough for your work. There are, however, a couple of important considerations specific to college. Portability and battery life are paramount. Regardless of your budget, you want something that will last throughout the day and won't weigh you down while you carry it from class to class. Anything more than 4 pounds will start to feel noticeable in your backpack.

Overall dimensions are important, too. Bringing a 16-inch laptop to class can feel obtuse, given the size of small desks. The same is true if you plan on bringing your laptop to a crowded coffee shop or library. That’s why 13- or 14-inch laptops are preferred. There are even 14-inch gaming laptops, such as the Razer Blade 14, that provide the discrete GPU performance you need without sacrificing portability.

Here are some other specs to consider:

Processor

- Windows: If you’re getting a Windows machine, your main options for the processor are Intel or Qualcomm. Both have strengths and weaknesses, but getting a Snapdragon X laptop ensures that you get really solid battery life. See our full guide to buying a laptop for more info.
- Chromebooks: These browser-based machines use half a dozen processors, most of which you’ve probably never heard of. There’s a reason for that: Those processors are slow. My recommendation when buying a Chromebook is to stick with a Chromebook Plus machine. This is a new standard Google created to ensure a certain level of performance and polish.
- MacOS: Apple has been making its own processors for a few years, like the latest M5 chip found inside the latest MacBook Pro. These more powerful MacBook Pros feature integrated GPUs that aim to be comparable with the discrete GPUs you find in Windows laptops. Our MacBook buying guide can help further.

RAM and Storage

Regardless of which OS you choose, the minimum amount of RAM you want in your laptop is 8 GB. That’s enough memory to keep your computer feeling snappy even if it’s running under load. But these days 16 GB is standard, and you’ll find lots of laptops around $800 or less that come with 16 GB. So, if you can afford it—especially if you plan to edit photos or videos as part of your coursework—go for a 16-GB or even 32-GB model.

The new default for storage is 256 GB, and it’ll do if you’re trying to save money. You can always use external storage if you need to add on. Spring for 512 GB or a terabyte if you can, though.

Screen

Screens vary tremendously, but don’t settle for anything less than 1080p (or 1200p for 16:10 aspect ratio displays). For a 13-inch laptop, 1080p is sharp enough. If you’re going with a bigger laptop, 2.5K or even 4K screens will improve the viewing experience. If you’re trying to play games as well, be sure to get something with a higher refresh rate— 120 Hz or 144 Hz will more than satisfy.

Weight and Battery

Don’t forget you’ll be lugging this thing around. It may be tugging on your back for eight hours or more. At the end of a long day of walking, you will likely notice the difference between a 3-pound and 4-pound laptop. Trust me. Also, consider picking out a nice bag to carry your computer in.

Similarly, battery life is very important when you’re (potentially) away from a wall outlet for extended periods. Whatever you end up getting, make sure it’s capable of lasting at least eight hours under real-world use—browsing the web, editing documents, writing emails, and taking notes. Even then, you might want to consider a portable battery charger.

Yes, for most college students, Chromebooks are a good option. They are cheaper than MacBooks or Windows laptops, and the Chromebook Plus models offer reliable performance at an affordable price. If your budget is $500 or less, things can get more iffy, but I’ve tested a couple of good options that I recommend in this guide in that price range.

Furthermore, you can run almost all apps in the web these days (including Office 365), and Android apps do a good job of filling in the gaps. Occasionally, though, you may run into some compatibility problems, whether with software or hardware. If you’re in a STEM, art, or design program, however, a Chromebook is probably not a good fit. For example, if you’re required to use CAD or Photoshop, you’ll want a Windows laptop.
